current_episode.title: Doula Life: What It’s Really Like to Be a Birth Doula

guest.bio_context: Mary Riley has supported over 2,500 births throughout her 39-year career as a doula, starting after attending seven friends' births in one summer. She began her practice 39 years ago in the Hudson Valley area after obtaining her doula certification through weekend workshops and book learning. She has also worked as a midwife assistant at a freestanding birth center in Athens and has collaborated with home birth midwives throughout her career.

context.real_quote: They have to walk away from this birth looking at each other and hopefully say, look at what we did together, because we have to parent and raise this child for the rest of our lives.
key_stats: 39 years of practice as a doula, starting 39 years ago after attending seven friends' births in one summer
Over 2,500 births supported by Mary Riley
Beginning doula fees: a few hundred dollars to cover costs like childcare and gas
Rural and suburban doula fees: $1,500 to a couple thousand dollars per birth
New York City doula fees: $3,000 to $4,000 per birth
Doula stay duration during labor: 10 to 50 hours depending on the birth
Post-birth support: 2 to 3 hours immediately after birth, plus 1 to 2 home visits

pending_qa.q: How much can a beginning doula earn, and what is the typical fee range by experience level?
pending_qa.r: Beginning doulas might charge a few hundred dollars, primarily to cover costs like childcare and gas, or even do births for free to gain education. As experience grows, doulas in rural and suburban areas outside major cities typically earn between $1,500 to a couple thousand dollars per birth. In New York City, doulas can charge $3,000 to $4,000 per birth, though Mary Riley does not work in the city.

pending_qa.q: At what stage of pregnancy does a doula typically begin working with a client?
pending_qa.r: Mary Riley meets with the mother, partner, and any family members who will be present, and once everyone is comfortable with each other, the doula begins support. Clients currently book her months in advance—she mentioned having clients booked into July while it is still January. She sees most clients two or three more times during pregnancy and stays in contact via phone calls and texts whenever the client has appointments, ultrasounds, or questions.

pending_qa.q: What is the biggest challenge of working as a doula?
pending_qa.r: Being on call is the hardest part of the job. It makes it difficult to plan personal activities and vacations because a birth can happen at any time, sometimes during scheduled time off. This lifestyle commitment means doulas must always be available, which requires backup doulas for emergency situations when the primary doula cannot be reached.

pending_qa.q: How do doulas work alongside hospital staff like nurses, midwives, and doctors?
pending_qa.r: Years ago, Mary Riley faced significant resistance from hospital staff who did not recognize the doula role and even threw her out of hospitals. However, over time and through building trust with midwives and doctors, she developed collaborative relationships. Now she advocates for clients by learning each hospital's current rules, which change frequently, and helping clients communicate effectively with healthcare providers rather than approaching the birth as a confrontation. She emphasizes that all roles—doula, nurse, midwife, doctor—are important and work best as a team.

pending_qa.q: What happens if a baby is born unexpectedly outside a hospital or birth center?
pending_qa.r: Mary Riley has caught babies in emergency situations, including one recent birth on the Rhinecliffe Bridge where the mother's water broke in a car stuck in back-to-back traffic. She instructed the father to sing to calm himself and coached the mother to catch her own baby. The baby did not cry immediately, so Mary told the father to keep singing and had the mother place the baby skin-to-skin and pat the baby's back to clear the lungs. The baby then screamed and they proceeded to the birth center.

pending_qa.q: How does a doula support partners and fathers during birth?
pending_qa.r: Mary Riley helps partners and fathers feel included and confident by keeping them connected to the mother, which keeps everyone calmer. She sometimes massages the father's shoulders and reminds him that what is happening is normal and okay, especially since many fathers have never witnessed birth before and may be frightened by the intensity of the mother's sounds and physical responses. She ensures the partner understands his important role and gives him credit for managing sleep loss, stress, and learning how to advocate.

pending_qa.q: Do doulas continue supporting families after the birth?
pending_qa.r: Yes. Mary Riley stays for two to three hours after the birth—whether at home or hospital—to make sure everyone is settled, the baby has begun breastfeeding if desired, and the mother and partner are fed and comfortable. She then does one or two home visits after they return home to help with breastfeeding and ensure everything is progressing well. For home births, she coordinates with the home birth midwives and visits between their home visits.

pending_qa.q: Why do families hire a doula for second and third births if they already have birth experience?
pending_qa.r: Families book Mary Riley for subsequent births because they feel connected and want the same emotional and practical support they had with their first birth. Although some assume experienced mothers will be fine on their own, Mary emphasizes that women having second and third babies deserve the same level of support as first-time mothers, and a doula can genuinely help.
